As South Korea industrializes more and more, the demand for industrial robotics has more than quadrupled over the last 15 years to reach over $2.3 billion helping total robotics sales reach $25 billion. The KIRIA has helped foster the South Korean robotics industry by appropriating R&D funds to various South Korean robotics endeavors. These grants have increased from $20 million to $40 million over the last several years. In addition, several major South Korean companies have been investing more into robotics research and development. Leading the way in innovation are Hyundai, Daewoo, and Samsung's robotics divisions. KIRIA has estimated that South Korean robotics have now recently caught up to the level of technology seen in the US, Japan, and Europe. This comes 7 years after their previous evaluation of South Korean robotics being 2-3 years behind.

Hyundai's robotics divisions have been supplying many industries around the world with various industrial robotic arms that perform tasks such as welding, cutting, material handling, sealing, palletizing, and more. Hyundai is fighting to compete with the more established industrial robotics companies such as Japan's Fanuc, Kawasaki, and Motoman and Europe's Kuka and ABB. Hyundai also teamed up with the Asan Institute for Life Sciences to advance it's medical robotics division.

Daewoo Shipbuilding and Marine Engineering has been working for several years on various prototype for exoskeletons that assist in lifting the heavy parts and tools in shipbuilding. Initial robo-suits had lifting capacity of 30 kg and were relatively slow. The latest suits have achieved lifting capacity of more than 100 kg pounds and are capable of moving much faster than the early prototypes. These suits have aided DSME to increase productivity and complete its many contracts quicker. Daewoo has announced that in 2022, they will spinoff the robot suit division to begin marketing the suits for commercial production both domestically and abroad.

Samsung's robotics divisions have been focusing on humanoid robots, domestic robotic applications such as robotic vacuum cleaners and military applications such as the Samsung SGR-A1, a robotic machine gun sentry that has been deployed to the DMZ to protect against the threat of North Korean aggression and to Iraq to guard South Korean bases.

Researchers at Chonnam National University have made great advancements in nanorobotics. Their Bacteriobot is based on a bacteria that has been engineered to identifying cancerous cells and deliver drugs directly those cells without harming healthy cells and contributing to the many side effects of traditional chemotherapy. Initial animal trials proved successful in demonstrating the efficacy of this technology. Human trials have recently begun and results are expected to be shared with the Netherlands Cancer Institute as South Korea works more closely with Dutch researchers to battle cancer.
[EVENT] Korea Institute for Robot Industry Advancement (KIRIA) Reports on 2021 Status of Korean Robotics: industrial, medical, and personal robots, industrial exoskeletons
The Dutch Cancer institute is anxiously looking forward to test results with the new Bacteriobots and hopes this will lead to a next gen in battling cancer.
